quotes.note: The controlling diary narrator uses “me” and “I” in a story-specific declaration about her own fate.
The narrator participates as “I” while assessing her students and stating her conviction.
The first-person possessive “my” identifies the narrator as the character whose plans have gone awry.
Repeated narratorial “I” statements describe the protagonist-narrator’s beliefs, desires, and mission.
The participating narrator uses “I” to report her own habitual physical reaction.
This is an impersonal gnomic assertion without diagnostic evidence about the story’s narrator.
The narrator recounts her own quest and transformations through “my” and repeated “I” constructions.
Myra explicitly identifies herself as “I” and narrates her purported past actions in the controlling diary voice.

web_evidence.title: Bodies That Do Not Fit: Sexual Metamorphoses, Re-embodied Identities and Cultural Crisis in Contemporary Transgender Memoirs
web_evidence.note: Anna Kérchy’s scholarly analysis explicitly identifies Myra’s account as a first-person singular diary narrative and describes the other constitutive chapters as transcriptions of Uncle Buck’s first-person Dictaphone monologues.

web_evidence.title: Myra Breckinridge Analysis
web_evidence.note: The structural analysis says the novel combines multiple first-person narrators: Myra’s diary entries and Buck Loner’s transcribed tape recordings.

web_evidence.title: 10 Best Hollywood Novels
web_evidence.note: The article explicitly characterizes Myra’s voice as first-person narration, though it does not discuss the Buck Loner interludes.

web_evidence.title: Myra Breckinridge by Gore Vidal
web_evidence.note: The publisher reproduces the first-person opening and calls it Myra’s testimony; this establishes the opening voice but not the whole-book structure.

web_evidence.title: A Phantasmic Woman
web_evidence.note: The critical review identifies Myra as the novel’s unreliable narrator and explains that readers are encountering diary entries she writes for her psychoanalyst.

search_log: Searched “Myra Breckinridge” with “first person,” “narrator,” “point of view,” and “diary narration.”
Searched for Gore Vidal excerpts, first chapters, publisher pages, Google Books previews, and Buck Loner’s recorded sections.
Opened the Penguin Random House edition page, Google Books record, Publishers Weekly article, Bookforum review, eNotes structural analysis, and the University of Szeged-hosted scholarly PDF.
Targeted searches for scholarly discussion found the Szeged analysis and an Edinburgh thesis result; the Edinburgh repository page failed to open and was not used as evidence.
Google Books exposed the opening and contents but not enough sustained interior prose to establish the whole structure independently.
person_note: The Goodreads passages repeatedly expose Myra’s participating first-person diary voice. Whole-book structural research shows that the novel also contains Buck Loner’s Dictaphone-report chapters, but these are another participating first-person voice rather than third-person narration. The Myra-to-Myron identity development likewise does not change narrative person. Under the methodology, multiple first-person narrators remain FIRST, not ALTERNATING. The quote sample contains only Myra’s strand, but the scholarly structural source accounts for Buck’s interludes, and no sustained second- or third-person base section was found.
